_tooltips.id: Unique within your organization and used verbatim in the application's URL. Short, lower-case and hyphenated, e.g. claims-app; avoid changing it later. — Guide: Application

_tooltips.description: A note for you and your fellow designers; users do not see it. — Guide: Application
_tooltips.status: DRAFT until the definition is published, PUBLISHED afterwards. Set by the system. — Guide: Save, preview and publish
_tooltips.version: Increases with every save. Set by the system. — Guide: Save, preview and publish
_tooltips.publishedVersion: The version users currently get. Changes only when you press Publish. — Guide: Save, preview and publish
_tooltips.updatedAt: When the definition was last saved. Set by the system.

_tooltips.sidenavCollapsible: Whether users can close the navigation panel. — Guide: Layout

_tooltips.routes: The pages of the application, one row per page. Add them before the navigation items that point at them. — Guide: Routes
_tooltips.modules: Separately authored parts of the application whose routes appear under a base path. — Guide: Modules

_tooltips.type: header (top), sidenav (navigation panel) or footer (bottom). Each type can be used once. — Guide: Regions
_tooltips.navItems: The menu entries of the sidenav. Used only by the sidenav region. — Guide: Navigation items
_tooltips.widgets: The widgets of the header or footer, laid out in one row in this order. Use a spacer to push the following ones to the right. — Guide: Header

_tooltips.translocoId: Optional translation key of the title, shown instead of it in other languages. — Guide: Routes
_tooltips.icon: A Material or FontAwesome icon name. — Guide: Routes
_tooltips.roles: The roles allowed to open this page; empty means any signed-in member of your organization. Not enforced yet. — Guide: Roles

concepts.title: How a dynamic application is put together
concepts.intro: An Application in ProcessPuzzle is not programmed — it is described. Everything you enter here (the frame, the menu, the pages and what each page shows) is stored as data, and the application shell builds the running application from that description at run time. Changing the application means editing its definition and publishing it again; nothing has to be rebuilt or redeployed.

assembling.title: Assembling your application, step by step
assembling.body:
1. Create the application — give it an Id and a Name.
  2. Choose its look — a Material theme, a colour scheme and a layout preset.
  3. Add the pages — one Route per page, and decide what each one renders: widgets, an entity or a document.
  4. Build the frame — add the header, sidenav and footer regions; fill the header and footer with widgets and the sidenav with navigation items pointing at your routes.
  5. Check it on the Preview tab.
  6. Publish it, so that users get the new version.

Routes come before navigation on purpose: a navigation item points at a route by its path, so it is easiest to write once the route exists.

application.title: Application
application.body: The top-level record that holds everything else. Its Id is unique within your organization and is used verbatim in the application's URL, so pick a short, lower-case, hyphenated value such as claims-app and avoid changing it later. The Name is what users see, for example in the app-title widget; the optional Transloco Id is a translation key used instead of the Name when the application is shown in other languages. The Description is for you and your fellow designers.

theme.title: Theme
theme.body:
Decides the colours of the whole application.

  • Material Theme — processpuzzle is the brand look and the default; the others are Angular Material palettes, and each of them recolours the header, sidenav, cards and buttons as well.
  • Color Scheme — light, dark, or auto (follows the user's operating system).
  • Logo Url and Favicon Url — the images shown by the app-logo widget and in the browser tab.
  • Token Overrides — fine-tuning on top of the theme: a --pp-… colour token and its value, e.g. --pp-surface-sidenav → #0d1b2a.

What you choose here is the application's default. If you place a themes-button widget in the header, each user can pick a theme of their own, which is then remembered for them.

layout.title: Layout
layout.body:
Decides where the regions sit around the pages.

  • Layout Preset — sidenav-left or sidenav-right put the navigation in a side panel; top-nav puts it in the header row instead.
  • Sidenav Mode — side keeps the panel beside the page, over lays it over the page, push slides the page aside while the panel is open.
  • Sidenav Collapsible / Sidenav Open By Default — whether users can close the panel, and whether it starts open.
  • Content Max Width — a CSS length such as 1280px that keeps pages readable on wide screens; empty means full width.

regions.title: Regions — the frame around the pages
regions.body: A region is a fixed part of the screen that stays in place while users move between pages. There are three types, and an application has at most one of each: header (top), sidenav (the navigation panel) and footer (bottom). Header and footer contain widgets; the sidenav contains navigation items. The area in the middle is not a region: it shows whichever route the user is on. A region you leave out simply does not appear.

header.title: Header
header.body: The bar across the top of the application. Its widgets are laid out in one row, left to right, in the order they are listed. Typical content is app-logo and app-title on the left, a spacer that pushes everything after it to the right, and a themes-button at the far right. The logo and title are ordinary widgets that read the application's Logo Url and Name, so you decide whether and where they appear. With the top-nav layout the navigation items are shown in the header row as well.

footer.title: Footer
footer.body: The bar across the bottom of the application. It works exactly like the header — a row of widgets in the order listed, with a spacer to push them apart — and is a good place for copyright notes, contact details or links. It stays at the bottom of the screen even when a page is short.

navigation.title: Navigation items
navigation.body: The entries of the menu, added to the sidenav region. Each one has a Label (optionally translated through its Transloco Id), an Icon (a Material or FontAwesome icon name) and a Route: the Path of the route it opens, written exactly as on the route, e.g. claims/open. An item without a route is a group: it opens and closes the items you add under its Children, so menus can be nested. A path that names no route yet is only a warning — it may belong to a module that has not been written yet.

routes.title: Routes — the pages
routes.body:
Every page of the application is a route.

  • Path — the page's address relative to the application, without a leading slash: claims, claims/open. A :name segment is a parameter, e.g. claims/:id.
  • Title, Transloco Id and Icon — how the page is named and shown.
  • Renders — what the page shows: WIDGETS, ENTITY or DOCUMENT. The fields below it apply to the chosen kind only.

Routes are a flat list. You never nest them by hand: claims and claims/open are two separate entries, and the shell works out from their paths that one lies under the other.

widgets.title: Widgets — the building blocks
widgets.body:
A widget is a ready-made piece of user interface — a logo, a title, a spacer, a theme picker, a grid of entities, a document viewer and more. Widgets are used in the header and the footer, and on WIDGETS routes, where they are stacked one under the other. The order in the list is the order on the screen.

  • Id — unique within its page or region, e.g. widget-claims-grid.
  • Type — which widget it is; only the widgets available in this installation are offered.
  • Props — the widget's settings. The form adapts to the chosen type and shows only the settings that type understands.
  • Placement — STANDALONE widgets are shown where they are listed. A container widget (such as a card grid) arranges other widgets by listing their ids in its props; mark those as REFERENCED, so they appear inside the container and not a second time on their own.

entities.title: Entities — data pages without design work
entities.body:
An ENTITY route shows one kind of business data — claims, customers, orders — without any page having to be designed. Set Entity Name to the name of an entity defined under Entities in the designer, and the framework generates a searchable list and a details form for it from the entity's attributes, together with the validation rules defined for it. From there users open, create, edit and delete records.

Entity Mode (LIST or DETAILS) and Rsql Filter (a pre-filter such as status==OPEN) are stored with the route but not applied yet: the page currently always opens on the full list.

documents.title: Documents
documents.body: A DOCUMENT route shows a document — content composed of text, images, data values and widgets, authored in the Documents designer. Set Document Slug to the slug of the document. Rendering a document as a page is not available yet, so the Preview shows a short notice in its place; to show document content today, use a WIDGETS route with a document-viewer widget.

modules.title: Modules
modules.body: A larger application can be split into modules. A module is authored separately, under Modules, and holds routes of its own; its Key must not change once the module is in use. An application includes a module through a Module Mount: Module Key names the module, and Base Path is the prefix its routes appear under — mounting a module under claims turns its route open into claims/open. A module cannot mount other modules; one level is all there is.

roles.title: Roles
roles.body: Routes and navigation items can name the Roles allowed to use them. Leaving the list empty means any signed-in member of your organization. Roles are stored with the definition, but the Preview does not restrict anything by them yet.

lifecycle.title: Save, preview and publish
lifecycle.body: A new application starts as a Draft. Save stores your changes; the Preview tab then shows the saved definition exactly as the running application renders it, theme included — check it there before going further. Publish makes the saved version the Published Version, the one users get. You can keep editing and saving afterwards; users see the changes only once you publish again.
